analysis.one_liner: Cancels all outstanding federal and private student loan debt.
analysis.headline: The bill to erase all federal and private student debt sat in three House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the full balance — principal and interest — of every federal student loan, including parent and consolidation loans, and would have the Department of Education buy private student loans from lenders at full value and cancel them too. Borrowers would get refunds for payments made after the bill became law, and none of the forgiven debt would count as taxable income. It was referred to three committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40-plus million Americans with outstanding federal or private student loans would have their entire balance erased at no cost to them, including parents who borrowed for their children's education and borrowers who took out high-interest private loans. Payments made after the law passed would be refunded.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All federal and private student loan borrowers

how_it_helps.text: The Department of Education must forgive the full outstanding principal and interest on all federal student loans — including Family Federal Education Loans, Direct Loans, Perkins Loans, parent loans, consolidation loans, and certain grants treated as loans — within 180 days of enactment.

The Department of Education would buy private student loans from private lenders — paying the unpaid principal, accrued interest, and late charges in full — and then cancel the debt, so private-loan borrowers are discharged with no out-of-pocket cost.
Forgiven amounts and post-enactment refunds are excluded from taxable income, so borrowers would not face a surprise tax bill on the cancelled debt.

Borrowers who keep paying between enactment and forgiveness get those payments refunded, and the bill requires plain-language public notice so borrowers know how to apply for the private-loan forgiveness.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the full cost of paying off federal loans and purchasing private loans from lenders at face value — a cost in the trillions of dollars. Current and future students would continue to borrow under the same system, and the bill does nothing to lower college prices or prevent new debt from piling up.

drawbacks.text: The benefit would be skewed toward households with larger balances, which tend to be higher-income graduate and professional degree holders, while lower-income Americans who never attended college get nothing.

The bill pays private lenders the full unpaid principal, interest, and late charges with no discount, so investors who bought high-interest private student debt would be made whole at taxpayer expense rather than sharing in any loss.
The bill is a one-time erasure of existing debt; it does nothing to change tuition levels or lending practices, so new borrowers would continue to accumulate debt under the same system.

The cost — cancelling all federal and private student debt at once with no income limits — is enormous and would fall on taxpayers, including people who never borrowed or who already paid off their loans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to borrowers would be life-changing and immediate: millions of households would see their largest monthly obligation disappear. But the bill was designed with no income limits, no discount when buying private loans from lenders, and no reform of college costs, so its cost to taxpayers would be maximized while the root problem — rising tuition and easy borrowing — would continue. A more targeted design could deliver much of the relief at a fraction of the cost, which was the strongest objection to the full-cancellation approach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the Student Debt Cancellation Act of 2019 on June 24, 2019, joined by eight original cosponsors including Reps. Jayapal, Tlaib, and Ocasio-Cortez.

The same day, the House referred the bill to the Education and Labor, Financial Services, and Ways and Means committees — a three-committee referral that means no single panel owns it and each can hold it indefinitely.
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll-call, for the remainder of the 116th Congress.
The bill never reached the Senate; it died with the Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan borrowers continue owing what they owed; private student lenders keep collecting interest on their loans rather than being paid off by the government; the Education Department never had to fund the cancellation. The members and committee chairs who left the bill unconsidered avoided a costly vote they did not have to take.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders keep collecting; borrowers keep owing

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cancel all federal and private student debt.

for.name: 15 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Jayapal, Tlaib, Jackson Lee, Norton, Lee of California, Garcia of Illinois, and Ocasio-Cortez.

against.name: House committee leadership (Education and Labor; Financial Services; Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on the bill during the two-year Congress; the record shows no action after the June 2019 referral.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: The bill never reached the House floor in the full two-year Congress; majority leadership, which controls scheduling, never brought it to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it, but the decisive step was inaction by the Democratic majority itself — the bill never got far enough for any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and holders (banks, finance companies, loan investors)
industries.note: The bill would have paid private lenders the full unpaid principal, interest, and late charges on eligible private student loans — making them whole at taxpayer expense — while discharging borrowers. Because the bill died, lenders continue collecting on those loans instead.

industries.industry: Federal loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Mass cancellation of federal loan balances would have eliminated the servicing fee and collection revenue tied to those loans. The bill's death preserved that revenue stream.
Had it passed, taxpayers would have funded the full cost of forgiving every federal loan and buying out private loans at face value, with no income limits. The bill's failure avoided that cost.
